extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions (readers of Tocqueville)
extracted.subtask_short: assessing democratic government strengths and weaknesses
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative standards for judging how democratic governments (with emphasis on the United States) perform in war, lawmaking, foreign policy, and social development. Focuses on capacities, weaknesses, and the conditions under which democracy yields advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for sustained effort (war/long contests)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to say what degree of exertion a democratic government may be capable of making at a crisis in the history of the nation; democracies show enthusiasm at the commencement of war but grow indifferent toward its close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American Revolutionary War showed early zeal but later private egoism, empty treasuries, difficulty raising recruits; sustained large-scale wars in other countries (England, France) required placing large shares of income or population at the government's disposal — tests democracies may find hard to meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of conscription/impressment in a democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the use of conscription is unknown and men are induced to enlist by bounties; the notions and habits of the people are opposed to compulsory enlistments and impressment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Without conscription or impressment it is hard to sustain a great continental or maritime war; the U.S. navy remained small and its vessels expensive to equip. Historical note: some US states experimented with classing/ballot substitution (1814) but experience was limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy better at occasional vigor than prolonged endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy appears much better adapted for the peaceful conduct of society, or for an occasional effort of remarkable vigor, than for the hardy and prolonged endurance of storms which beset the political existence of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: enthusiasm prompts immediate bravery, but perseverance requires reflection and a distinct perception of the future, which democracies more often lack; lower classes suffer more acutely from privations than nobles, reducing sustained sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of the people to feel rather than to reason (affects perseverance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The populace is more apt to feel than to reason; if present sufferings are great, it is to be feared the still greater sufferings attendant upon defeat will be forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: democratic publics may accept short-term measures motivated by passion and then abandon long-term prudent courses; this undermines long perseverance in policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control and acquiescence in what benefits interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The American People acquiesces slowly, or frequently does not acquiesce in what is beneficial to its interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative consequence: because legislation is made by and for the people, laws may favor classes interested in evading them; politically costly measures (e.g., duties on brandy, strict bankruptcy penalties) are hard to enact because of majority resistance and electoral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws reflect ends vs means distinction (democratic laws' relative excellence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering laws one must distinguish between the end at which they aim and the means by which they are directed to that end; democratic laws generally tend to promote the welfare of the greatest possible number, but their means are often imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: a law well drawn to favor a bad end can be effective and harmful; democracies aim at majority welfare (a beneficial end) yet often have ineffective or inopportune means compared with aristocracies, which are more expert in legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of democracy to learn and repair faults by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The great privilege of the Americans consists in their being able to repair the faults they may commit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracies can regain the right path after errors because they are less encumbered by entrenched internal interests; this corrective ability depends on time and the population's capacity to learn from experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a certain level of education and civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy cannot derive substantial benefit from past experience unless it be arrived at a certain pitch of knowledge and civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples: tribes or peoples with vicious education and a mixture of passion and ignorance cannot discern remedies and perish despite obvious remedies; South American provinces' recurring revolutions illustrate inability to profit from experience without sufficient civic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic public officers' interests aligned with majority
rubrics_metrics.description: In the American democracy public officers have no permanent interests distinct from those of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: although democratic magistrates may be less honest or capable, the electorate's vigilance, short tenures, and prevention of divergence between rulers' interests and the public good help states to prosper despite imperfect rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign policy requires qualities democracies lack
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign politics demand scarcely any of the qualities which a democracy possesses; they require, on the contrary, the perfect use of almost all those faculties in which it is deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required qualities: ability to regulate details of important undertakings, to persevere in a design, to work out execution amidst obstacles, to combine measures with secrecy, and to await consequences with patience. Examples: Washington and Jefferson's maxims of neutrality; popular passions during the French Revolution threatened to drive the U.S. into imprudent war absent Washington's steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's internal advantages (resources, public spirit, respect for law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy is favorable to the increase of the internal resources of a state; it tends to diffuse a moderate independence; it promotes the growth of public spirit, and fortifies the respect which is entertained for law in all classes of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These internal benefits indirectly improve relations among nations but do not substitute for the specific skills required by foreign policy or grand long-term undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy's comparative strengths (expertise, perseverance, fixity of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracies are infinitely more expert in the science of legislation than democracies; they possess a self-control which protects them from errors of temporary excitement and form lasting designs matured with favorable opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: aristocracies can combine laws to concentrate force at the right time and thus more readily conceive and execute vast designs that lead to predominant international positions; democracies lack this fixity and secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity of democracies to follow passion over prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity which democracies have to obey the impulse of passion rather than the suggestions of prudence, and to abandon a mature design for the gratification of a momentary caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: during the French Revolution American popular sympathies risked dragging the nation into a war contrary to its interests; only Washington's character prevented imprudent national action. Democratic leaders therefore face the danger of losing majority support when opposing popular emotion.
